hints: Think about the job of the final hybridoma cell. It needs two superpowers: to make one specific antibody, and to divide forever in culture. Which normal cell can do each job?
Remember which lymphocyte actually secretes antibody (plasma B-cell, not T-cell) and which abnormal cell divides uncontrollably to give immortality in culture.
walkthrough:
**Recall what we want to make**

Great start. We want lots of identical, specific antibody from cells that will live and divide forever in the lab.

No single normal cell can do both jobs, so we have to combine them.

**Match each job to a cell**

The antibody-making expert is the activated B-lymphocyte called the plasma cell. It makes the exact antibody we want, but it dies quickly in culture.

The divide-forever expert is a myeloma cell, a type of cancer cell. It does not make the wanted antibody, but it is immortal in culture.

**Name the fusion product**

When we fuse these two cells together, we get a hybridoma cell. It inherits both talents: specific antibody production plus unlimited mitosis.

That is why the two structures fused are cancer cells and plasma cells, option C.

options.A: Antigens are not fused. They are injected into a mouse first to stimulate plasma cells, and hybridoma cells are the result of fusion, not a starting material.
options.B: T-lymphocytes do not secrete antibodies, they are involved in cell-mediated immunity. We need antibody-secreting plasma (B) cells for this technique.
options.C: Correct. An antibody-secreting plasma cell is fused with an immortal myeloma cancer cell to form an antibody-producing, continuously dividing hybridoma.
options.D: Hybridoma cells are produced after fusion, not fused, and antibodies are the secreted product, not a cell to fuse.
